claim: In 2023, about 19,710 new cases of ovarian cancer (OC) will be diagnosed in the United States.
source: The American Cancer Society estimates that in 2023, about 19,710 new cases of ovarian cancer (OC) will be diagnosed and about 13,270 individuals will die from OC in the United States (Cancer Facts & Figures 2022, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cancer Facts & Figures 2022

claim: About 13,270 individuals will die from ovarian cancer in the United States in 2023.
source: The American Cancer Society estimates that in 2023, about 19,710 new cases of ovarian cancer (OC) will be diagnosed and about 13,270 individuals will die from OC in the United States (Cancer Facts & Figures 2022, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cancer Facts & Figures 2022

claim: The mortality rate for ovarian cancer has declined only slightly in the last 40 years.
source: Unlike most other cancers, the mortality rate for OC has declined only slightly in the last 40 years due to lack of early diagnostic tests and effective treatments.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about ovarian cancer mortality trends

claim: The 5-year survival rate for all types of ovarian cancer averages 49.7%.
source: The 5-year survival rate for all types of OC averages 49.7%, much lower than many other cancers (Cancer Stat Facts: Ovarian Cancer, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cancer Stat Facts: Ovarian Cancer, 2019

claim: The 5-year survival rate for ovarian cancer is much lower than many other cancers.
source: The 5-year survival rate for all types of OC averages 49.7%, much lower than many other cancers (Cancer Stat Facts: Ovarian Cancer, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cancer Stat Facts: Ovarian Cancer, 2019

claim: The high mortality rate of ovarian cancer is linked to a lack of understanding of ovarian carcinogenesis and precursor lesions.
source: The high mortality rate of OC is linked to a lack of understanding of ovarian carcinogenesis and precursor lesions, contributing to the failure of early detection and late-stage diagnosis.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the relationship between understanding disease mechanisms and clinical outcomes

claim: Ovarian carcinoma represents a heterogeneous collection of cancer subtypes, each with distinct origins and molecular drivers.
source: Even the cell origins of various OC subtypes have not been fully appreciated until recently, with ovarian carcinoma representing a heterogeneous collection of cancer subtypes, each with distinct origins and molecular drivers (Shih et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shih et al., 2021

claim: The fallopian tube epithelium is the likely origin of most high-grade serous carcinomas.
source: The fallopian tube (FT) epithelium is the likely origin of most high-grade serous carcinomas, the most common subtype of ovarian carcinoma.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about the origin of high-grade serous carcinomas

claim: High-grade serous carcinoma is the most common subtype of ovarian carcinoma.
source: The fallopian tube (FT) epithelium is the likely origin of most high-grade serous carcinomas, the most common subtype of ovarian carcinoma.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about ovarian cancer subtypes

claim: The fallopian tubes form a conduit between the lower genital tract and the pelvic cavity.
source: The FTs form a conduit between the lower genital tract and the pelvic cavity (Heller et al., 1996; Henderson et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heller et al., 1996 and Henderson et al., 1979

claim: Blocking the communication between the fallopian tubes and the environment through tubal ligation or hysterectomy results in lower ovarian cancer incidences.
source: Blocking the communication between the FTs and the environment, such as through tubal ligation or hysterectomy, results in lower OC incidences (Gaitskell et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Parker et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gaitskell et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Parker et al., 2009

claim: Increased cellular and bacterial transit between the lower genital tract and the peritoneal cavity, as in endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease, is associated with increased ovarian cancer risks.
source: Increased cellular and bacterial transit between the lower genital tract and the peritoneal cavity, as in endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease, is associated with increased OC risks (Melin et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Melin et al., 2011 and Lin et al., 2011

claim: Inhibiting ovulation through oral contraceptives may decrease ovarian cancer risks.
source: Inhibiting ovulation through oral contraceptives may decrease OC risks (Narod et al., 1998; Tworoger et al., 2007; Ness et al., 2001) by reducing the opportunities of incorporating ascending pathogens into the ovarian surface epithelium during ovulation-induced microtrauma.
evidence: Supported by citations to Narod et al., 1998; Tworoger et al., 2007; Ness et al., 2001

claim: Oral contraceptives may decrease ovarian cancer risks by reducing the opportunities of incorporating ascending pathogens into the ovarian surface epithelium during ovulation-induced microtrauma.
source: Inhibiting ovulation through oral contraceptives may decrease OC risks (Narod et al., 1998; Tworoger et al., 2007; Ness et al., 2001) by reducing the opportunities of incorporating ascending pathogens into the ovarian surface epithelium during ovulation-induced microtrauma.
evidence: Based on logical inference about the mechanism by which oral contraceptives reduce ovarian cancer risk

claim: The fallopian tubal epithelium has been implicated as the site of origin for at least a substantial proportion of high-grade serous carcinomas.
source: The fallopian tubal epithelium has been implicated in recent studies as the site of origin for at least a substantial proportion of high-grade serous carcinomas (Norquist et al., 2010; Medeiros et al., 2006; Lamb et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Norquist et al., 2010; Medeiros et al., 2006; Lamb et al., 2006

claim: Recent studies have demonstrated the presence of genital tract bacteria in the upper reproductive tract of women without known infections.
source: Furthermore, recent studies have demonstrated the presence of genital tract bacteria in the upper reproductive tract of women without known infections (Mitchell et al., 2015; Chambers et al., 2021; Walther-António et al., 2016; Ventolini et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 2015; Chambers et al., 2021; Walther-António et al., 2016; Ventolini et al., 2022

claim: Bacteria ascending from the lower genital tract may reside in the fallopian tubes and could induce a pro-inflammatory environment.
source: Therefore, bacteria ascending from the lower genital tract may reside in the FTs and could induce a pro-inflammatory environment, which could influence neoplasia of the tubal or ovarian epithelium, with outcome dependent on species of bacteria, concentration, host factors, and duration of exposure.
evidence: Involves hypothetical reasoning about the potential role of bacteria in the fallopian tubes

claim: A pro-inflammatory environment in the fallopian tubes could influence neoplasia of the tubal or ovarian epithelium.
source: Therefore, bacteria ascending from the lower genital tract may reside in the FTs and could induce a pro-inflammatory environment, which could influence neoplasia of the tubal or ovarian epithelium, with outcome dependent on species of bacteria, concentration, host factors, and duration of exposure.
evidence: Involves hypothetical reasoning about the potential role of inflammation in neoplasia

claim: Several studies have provided evidence that the fallopian tube may not be sterile.
source: Several studies have provided evidence that the FT may not be sterile (Miles et al., 2017; Brewster et al., 2022; Asangba et al., 2023), but rigorous controls and large sample sizes are needed to assess the microbiota in low-biomass samples.
evidence: Supported by citations to Miles et al., 2017; Brewster et al., 2022; Asangba et al., 2023

claim: A total of 187 patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria were enrolled in this study.
source: A total of 187 patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria (see Methods) were enrolled in this study.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript as a study characteristic

claim: The patient characteristics were different between the cancer and non-cancer patients in their age and menopausal status.
source: The patient characteristics were different between the cancer and non-cancer patients in their age and menopausal status as summarized in Table 1, with a higher percentage of the OC patients in the older and postmenopausal groups.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 1

claim: A higher percentage of ovarian cancer patients were in the older and postmenopausal groups compared to non-cancer patients.
source: The patient characteristics were different between the cancer and non-cancer patients in their age and menopausal status as summarized in Table 1, with a higher percentage of the OC patients in the older and postmenopausal groups.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 1

claim: Most ovarian cancers were diagnosed in stages III and IV.
source: Most OCs were diagnosed in stages III and IV, with high-grade serous carcinoma being the most common histology subtype (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 1

claim: High-grade serous carcinoma was the most common histology subtype among ovarian cancer patients in this study.
source: Most OCs were diagnosed in stages III and IV, with high-grade serous carcinoma being the most common histology subtype (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 1

claim: Laparotomy was more commonly performed in ovarian cancer patients.
source: Laparotomy was more commonly performed in OC patients (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 1

claim: Eight hundred and fifty-four biological samples and 147 non-biological laboratory controls were analyzed for microbiota composition.
source: Eight hundred and fifty-four biological samples and 147 non-biological laboratory controls were analyzed for microbiota composition (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated as a study characteristic

claim: Three hundred and sixty-nine swabs were collected from the fallopian tube and ovarian surfaces.
source: Three hundred and sixty-nine swabs were collected from the FT and ovarian surfaces.
evidence: Directly stated as a study characteristic

claim: 130 'air swabs' were collected from the patient's room to assess the microbial environment in the operating room.
source: To assess the microbial environment in the operating room, 130 'air swabs' were collected from the patient's room.
evidence: Directly stated as a study design element

claim: 152 cervical swabs were collected before surgical area preparation and vaginal sterilization to assess the cervical microbiota.
source: To assess the cervical microbiota, 152 cervical swabs were collected before surgical area preparation and vaginal sterilization.
evidence: Directly stated as a study design element

claim: 81 'laparoscopic port swabs' were collected after the port insertion and before the start of operation to assess the skin microbiota that may be introduced into the pelvic cavity during laparoscopic port insertion.
source: To assess the skin microbiota that may be introduced into the pelvic cavity during laparoscopic port insertion, 81 'laparoscopic port swabs' were collected after the port insertion and before the start of operation.
evidence: Directly stated as a study design element

claim: 122 'paracolic gutter swabs' were collected from the right paracolic gutter before the start of operation to assess the microbiota in the abdominal cavity away from the surgical or cancer sites.
source: To assess the microbiota in the abdominal cavity away from the surgical or cancer sites, 122 'paracolic gutter swabs' were collected from the right paracolic gutter before the start of operation.
evidence: Directly stated as a study design element

claim: 36 'buffer controls' containing only DNA extraction buffer without any swab or other DNA were included during each batch of DNA extractions to assess potential contamination of DNA extraction reagents.
source: To assess potential contamination of DNA extraction reagents, during each batch of DNA extractions we included 'buffer controls' that contained only DNA extraction buffer without any swab or other DNA. These 36 'buffer controls' were processed and then sequenced together with the swab samples.
evidence: Directly stated as a study design element

claim: 111 no-template PCR controls containing only PCR reagents and water without extracted DNA or buffer were included during each sequencing run to assess potential contamination during PCR and sequencing.
source: To assess potential contamination during PCR and sequencing, we also included multiple no-template PCR controls that contained only PCR reagents and water without extracted DNA or buffer (n = 111 total) during each sequencing run (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated as a study design element

claim: The bacterial concentrations of fallopian tube and ovarian surfaces averaged 2.5 copies of 16S rRNA genes/μl of DNA with a standard deviation of 4.6.
source: The bacterial concentrations of FT and ovarian surfaces averaged 2.5 copies of 16S rRNA genes/μl of DNA (standard deviation, 4.6).
evidence: Directly stated as a measurement result

claim: Fallopian tube and ovarian surface swabs contained higher concentrations of bacterial DNA than buffer controls and operating room air swabs (p-value <0.001).
source: Compared to the buffer controls and the OR air swabs, the FT and ovarian surface swabs contained higher concentrations of bacterial DNA than the controls (p-value <0.001) (Figure 1; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 2

claim: Cervical swabs contained thousands of times higher bacterial concentrations than fallopian tube and ovarian surface swabs (p-value <0.001).
source: As expected, the cervical swabs contained thousands of times higher bacterial concentrations than the FT and ovarian surface swabs (p-value <0.001) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 1

claim: The bacterial concentrations from the paracolic gutter were similar to those from the fallopian tube and ovarian surface swabs (p-value = 0.11).
source: The bacterial concentrations from the paracolic gutter were similar to those from the FT and ovarian surface swabs (p-value = 0.11) (Figure 1; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and data presented in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 2

claim: In the raw sequencing analysis, 892 bacterial species were present with at least 100 reads in at least one sample.
source: In the raw sequencing analysis, 892 bacterial species were present with at least 100 reads in at least one sample.
evidence: Directly stated as a sequencing analysis result

claim: After filtering, 84 bacterial species were present in at least one cervical and one fallopian tube sample with over 100 reads while not present in non-biological and air swabs.
source: After a series of filtering as described in Methods, 84 bacterial species were present in at least one cervical and one FT sample with over 100 reads while not present in non-biological and air swabs (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Directly stated as a filtering result

claim: These 84 bacterial species may represent the fallopian tube microbiota that are present in some women.
source: These 84 bacterial species may represent the FT microbiota that are present in some women.
evidence: Based on inference from the filtering and analysis results

claim: The Principle Component Analysis plot showed a high level of similarity between the fallopian tube/ovarian surface and the paracolic gutter swabs.
source: When analyzing the 340 samples that contained at least one read of these 84 species, the Principle Component Analysis (PCA) plot showed a high level of similarity between the fallopian tube/ovarian surface and the paracolic gutter swabs, indicating these species represent the shared microbiota community in the abdominal and pelvic cavity within each individual (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis and data presented in Figure 2A

claim: The 84 bacterial species represent the shared microbiota community in the abdominal and pelvic cavity within each individual.
source: When analyzing the 340 samples that contained at least one read of these 84 species, the Principle Component Analysis (PCA) plot showed a high level of similarity between the fallopian tube/ovarian surface and the paracolic gutter swabs, indicating these species represent the shared microbiota community in the abdominal and pelvic cavity within each individual (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on inference from the PCA analysis results

claim: Some bacterial species like Klebsiella or Anaerococcus are prevalent in multiple individuals.
source: An overview of these 84 bacterial species and their presence in each FT/ovarian surface sample shows that some of the bacterial species are prevalent in multiple individuals, such as Klebsiella or Anaerococcus, while others are only present in a few individuals, such as Casaltella or BV-associated bacterium 2 (BVAB2) (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 3

claim: Some bacterial species like Casaltella or BV-associated bacterium 2 (BVAB2) are only present in a few individuals.
source: An overview of these 84 bacterial species and their presence in each FT/ovarian surface sample shows that some of the bacterial species are prevalent in multiple individuals, such as Klebsiella or Anaerococcus, while others are only present in a few individuals, such as Casaltella or BV-associated bacterium 2 (BVAB2) (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 3

claim: Clustering did not identify any obvious groupings by processing batch, cancer status, menopausal status, or age for the putative fallopian tube bacterial species.
source: Clustering did not identify any obvious groupings by processing batch, cancer status, menopausal status, or age for these putative FT bacterial species (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis and data presented in Figure 3

claim: There were 726 bacterial species present in the cervix, fallopian tube/ovarian surface, and paracolic gutter after filtering out the bacteria present in no-template controls and DNA extraction controls.
source: There were 726 bacterial species present in the cervix, FT/ovarian surface, and paracolic gutter after filtering out the bacteria present in no-template controls and DNA extraction controls (i.e. after step #5 in Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Directly stated as a filtering result

claim: The cervical samples had lower Shannon diversity index than the fallopian tube/ovarian surface and paracolic gutter samples.
source: The cervical samples had lower Shannon diversity index than the FT/ovarian surface and paracolic gutter samples, while the non-cancer versus OC samples did not show any statistically significant difference in Shannon diversity within each sample type other than the cervical samples (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by Shannon diversity analysis and data presented in Figure 2B

claim: Non-cancer versus ovarian cancer samples did not show any statistically significant difference in Shannon diversity within each sample type other than the cervical samples.
source: The cervical samples had lower Shannon diversity index than the FT/ovarian surface and paracolic gutter samples, while the non-cancer versus OC samples did not show any statistically significant difference in Shannon diversity within each sample type other than the cervical samples (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by Shannon diversity analysis and data presented in Figure 2B

claim: Some bacteria, such as Streptococcus parasanguinis or Neisseriaceae, are more common in fallopian tube/ovarian surface samples from ovarian cancer patients.
source: Some bacteria, such as Streptococcus parasanguinis or Neisseriaceae, are more common in FT/ovarian surface samples from OC patients, while others (e.g. Ruminiclostridium, Dialister invisus, or Bacteroides dorei) are only present in OC patients albeit overall representation was low.
evidence: Supported by comparison analysis between cancer and non-cancer patients

claim: Some bacteria like Ruminiclostridium, Dialister invisus, or Bacteroides dorei are only present in ovarian cancer patients albeit overall representation was low.
source: Some bacteria, such as Streptococcus parasanguinis or Neisseriaceae, are more common in FT/ovarian surface samples from OC patients, while others (e.g. Ruminiclostridium, Dialister invisus, or Bacteroides dorei) are only present in OC patients albeit overall representation was low.
evidence: Supported by comparison analysis between cancer and non-cancer patients

claim: There is a clear shift in the microbiota of ovarian cancer patients when compared to non-cancer patients.
source: After ranking the FT bacteria based on the prevalence difference, we found a clear shift in the microbiota of the OC patients when compared to the non-cancer patients.
evidence: Based on inference from the prevalence difference analysis

claim: 90% of the top 20 species that were most prevalent in the fallopian tube of ovarian cancer patients were bacteria that predominantly exist outside the female reproductive tract.
source: Interestingly, 90% of the top 20 species that were most prevalent in the FT of OC patients were bacteria that predominantly exist outside the female reproductive tract.
evidence: Supported by prevalence analysis and categorization of bacterial species

claim: 60% of the top 20 species most prevalent in the fallopian tube of ovarian cancer patients predominantly reside in the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Among these, 12 (60%) predominantly reside in the gastrointestinal tract, such as Klebsiella, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Ruminiclostridium, and Roseburia.
evidence: Supported by prevalence analysis and categorization of bacterial species

claim: 30% of the top 20 species most prevalent in the fallopian tube of ovarian cancer patients normally reside in the mouth.
source: Six of the top 20 species (or 30%) normally reside in the mouth, such as Streptococcus mitis, Corynebacterium simulans/striatum, and D. invisus.
evidence: Supported by prevalence analysis and categorization of bacterial species

claim: Vaginal bacterial species, such as Corynebacterium amycolatum, Gardnerella, and Lactobacillus iners, are more prevalent in the fallopian tube from non-cancer patients.
source: On the contrary, vaginal bacterial species, such as Corynebacterium amycolatum, Gardnerella, and Lactobacillus iners, are more prevalent in the FT from non-cancer patients, representing 75% of the top 20 bacterial species that are most prevalent in non-cancer patients.
evidence: Supported by prevalence analysis and categorization of bacterial species

claim: Vaginal bacterial species represent 75% of the top 20 bacterial species that are most prevalent in non-cancer patients.
source: On the contrary, vaginal bacterial species, such as Corynebacterium amycolatum, Gardnerella, and Lactobacillus iners, are more prevalent in the FT from non-cancer patients, representing 75% of the top 20 bacterial species that are most prevalent in non-cancer patients.
evidence: Supported by prevalence analysis and categorization of bacterial species

claim: The pattern of bacterial prevalence was consistently observed in the paracolic gutter samples.
source: This pattern was also consistently observed in the paracolic gutter samples which share the same low-biomass environment of abdominal and pelvic cavity , suggesting that the above findings of FT microbiota were not random.
evidence: Supported by comparison of prevalence patterns across sample types

claim: The findings of fallopian tube microbiota were not random.
source: This pattern was also consistently observed in the paracolic gutter samples which share the same low-biomass environment of abdominal and pelvic cavity , suggesting that the above findings of FT microbiota were not random.
evidence: Based on inference from the consistency of patterns across sample types

claim: Serous carcinoma had higher prevalence of almost all 84 fallopian tube bacterial species compared to the other ovarian cancer subtypes.
source: When the histology subtypes were considered in the analysis, we found that the most common subtype, serous carcinoma, had higher prevalence of almost all 84 FT bacterial species compared to the other OC subtypes (Figure 5), indicating a higher level of perturbance in the FT microbiota in the serous carcinoma cases.
evidence: Supported by subtype analysis and data presented in Figure 5

claim: Serous carcinoma cases show a higher level of perturbance in the fallopian tube microbiota.
source: When the histology subtypes were considered in the analysis, we found that the most common subtype, serous carcinoma, had higher prevalence of almost all 84 FT bacterial species compared to the other OC subtypes (Figure 5), indicating a higher level of perturbance in the FT microbiota in the serous carcinoma cases.
evidence: Based on inference from the higher prevalence of bacterial species in serous carcinoma

claim: When only laparotomy cases were considered, the pattern of prevalence of majority of the 84 fallopian tube bacterial species was nearly identical as the overall comparison including all surgical types.
source: When only laparotomy cases were considered in the comparison of OC versus non-cancer patients, the pattern of prevalence of majority of the 84 FT bacterial species was nearly identical as the overall comparison including all surgical types (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by subgroup analysis presented in Supplementary file 4

claim: When laparotomy cases were compared to laparoscopic or robotic cases within the non-cancer patients, the prevalence of most of the 84 fallopian tube bacterial species was similar between the surgical types.
source: When laparotomy cases were compared to laparoscopic or robotic cases within the non-cancer patients, the prevalence of most of the 84 FT bacterial species was similar between the surgical types (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by subgroup analysis presented in Supplementary file 5

claim: The differences observed in the putative fallopian tube microbiota between ovarian cancer and non-ovarian cancer patients were not caused by the differences in surgical approaches.
source: These analyses demonstrate that the differences we observed in the putative FT microbiota between OC and non-OC patients were not caused by the differences in surgical approaches.
evidence: Based on inference from the surgical subgroup analyses

claim: 84 bacterial species are present in fallopian tube or ovarian surface, which may represent a fallopian tube microbiota in some women.
source: After detailed analyses and filtering out likely contaminants, we found 84 bacterial species that are present in FT or ovarian surface, which may represent an FT microbiota in some women.
evidence: Based on inference from the filtering and analysis results

claim: Comparison between ovarian cancer and non-cancer cases revealed a significantly higher prevalence of bacterial species that predominantly do not reside in the reproductive tract in patients with ovarian cancer.
source: Comparison between the OC and non-cancer cases revealed a significantly higher prevalence of bacterial species that predominantly do not reside in the reproductive tract in patients with OC, while the FT from non-cancer patients favored vaginal bacterial species.
evidence: Supported by comparison analysis between cancer and non-cancer patients

claim: The fallopian tube from non-cancer patients favored vaginal bacterial species.
source: Comparison between the OC and non-cancer cases revealed a significantly higher prevalence of bacterial species that predominantly do not reside in the reproductive tract in patients with OC, while the FT from non-cancer patients favored vaginal bacterial species.
evidence: Supported by comparison analysis between cancer and non-cancer patients

claim: It is unclear whether ovarian cancer leads to the microbiota shift or if the microbiota shift precedes ovarian cancer.
source: It is unclear whether OC leads to this microbiota shift or if the microbiota shift precedes OC.
evidence: Acknowledges the limitation of the cross-sectional study design in determining causality

claim: Bacterial species exist at a low concentration in the fallopian tube and ovarian surface in most women without overt signs of infection.
source: Our study showed the existence of bacterial species at a low concentration in the FT and ovarian surface in most women without overt signs of infection.
evidence: Supported by the bacterial concentration measurements and analysis

claim: Some bacterial species overlap between the fallopian tube and the cervical swabs, indicating potential ascension from the lower to the upper genital tract.
source: Some of these bacterial species overlapped between the FT and the cervical swabs, indicating potential ascension from the lower to the upper genital tract.
evidence: Based on inference from the overlap of bacterial species between sites

claim: Some bacterial species in the fallopian tube samples are not typical vaginal microbiota, and the origins of these bacteria are less clear.
source: Some other bacterial species are not typical vaginal microbiota, and the origins of these bacteria in the FT samples are less clear.
evidence: Based on inference from the categorization of bacterial species

claim: Patients with ovarian cancer, especially the serous carcinoma subtype, showed significantly higher prevalence of many of the bacterial species identified as the putative fallopian tube microbiota.
source: Patients with OC, especially the serous carcinoma subtype, showed significantly higher prevalence of many of the bacterial species we identified as the putative FT microbiota, indicating a potential link between a perturbed FT microbiota and OC.
evidence: Supported by prevalence analysis comparing cancer and non-cancer patients

claim: There is a potential link between a perturbed fallopian tube microbiota and ovarian cancer.
source: Patients with OC, especially the serous carcinoma subtype, showed significantly higher prevalence of many of the bacterial species we identified as the putative FT microbiota, indicating a potential link between a perturbed FT microbiota and OC.
evidence: Based on inference from the higher prevalence of bacterial species in ovarian cancer patients

claim: The fallopian tube microbiota may be different in different ovarian cancer histology subtypes.
source: The FT microbiota may be different in different OC histology subtype, which was consistent with a recent study with limited sample size (Asangba et al., 2023).
evidence: Based on inference from the subtype analysis and supported by citation to Asangba et al., 2023

claim: Most of the top bacterial species that were more prevalent in ovarian cancer patients had predominant niche outside of female reproductive tract, normally residing in the gastrointestinal or oral tract.
source: One of the most interesting findings from our study is that most of the top bacterial species that were more prevalent in OC patients had predominant niche outside of female reproductive tract, normally residing in the gastrointestinal or oral tract.
evidence: Supported by prevalence analysis and categorization of bacterial species

claim: Some bacterial species identified in this study were also identified in previous small studies examining the bacteria incorporated into the fallopian tube and ovarian cancer tissues, such as Anaerococcus, Klebsiella, Bacteroides, and Streptococcus.
source: Some of these bacterial species were also identified in previous small studies examining the bacteria incorporated into the FT and OC tissues, such as Anaerococcus, Klebsiella, Bacteroides, and Streptococcus (Asangba et al., 2023; Banerjee et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Asangba et al., 2023 and Banerjee et al., 2017

claim: The origin and route of ascension of gastrointestinal and oral bacteria to the fallopian tube and ovarian surfaces remain unknown.
source: The origin and route of ascension of these bacteria to the FT and ovarian surfaces remain unknown.
evidence: Acknowledges the limitation of the study in determining bacterial origins and routes

claim: In late-stage cancers, even when there are no overt signs of gastrointestinal invasion, the permeability of the intestinal tract may be increased which can increase the prevalence of gastrointestinal bacterial species in the fallopian tube, ovarian surfaces, and paracolic gutters.
source: In late-stage cancers, even when there are no overt signs of gastrointestinal invasion, the permeability of the intestinal tract may be increased which can increase the prevalence of these bacterial species in the FT, ovarian surfaces, and paracolic gutters.
evidence: Involves hypothetical reasoning about potential mechanisms

claim: The approach of collecting swabs in a sterile fashion in the operating room before the surgical case starts is unique and has not been used in previous studies.
source: Our approach in collecting swabs in a sterile fashion in the operating room before the surgical case starts is unique and has not been used in previous studies (Miles et al., 2017; Brewster et al., 2022; Asangba et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by comparison with previous studies cited

claim: The approach of collecting swabs in a sterile fashion enables evaluation of the microbiota in each individual patient at multiple sites to infer transfer among sites.
source: This approach enables us to evaluate the microbiota in each individual patient at multiple sites to infer transfer among sites.
evidence: Based on logical inference about the advantages of the study design

claim: Previous studies mostly used tissues collected from the pathology department after gross examination, which can introduce contamination.
source: Previous studies mostly used the tissues collected from the pathology department after gross examination, which can introduce contamination.
evidence: Based on knowledge of previous study methodologies and their limitations

claim: Previous studies infrequently included negative controls to assess for environmental or laboratory contamination.
source: These studies infrequently included negative controls to assess for environmental or laboratory contamination, which is critically important when assessing a low-biomass microbiome (Salter et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on knowledge of previous study methodologies and supported by citation to Salter et al., 2014

claim: Negative controls are critically important when assessing a low-biomass microbiome.
source: These studies infrequently included negative controls to assess for environmental or laboratory contamination, which is critically important when assessing a low-biomass microbiome (Salter et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Salter et al., 2014

claim: The biological controls and laboratory controls provide a fuller picture of the patient-specific microbiota and differentiate the biologically meaningful bacterial species from likely contaminants.
source: These biological controls, along with the DNA extraction and PCR controls during the sample processing and sequencing processes, provide a fuller picture of the patient-specific microbiota and differentiate the biologically meaningful bacterial species from likely contaminants.
evidence: Based on logical inference about the advantages of the study design

claim: The approach taken in this study may serve as a guide for others undertaking microbiome studies of low-biomass environments.
source: The approach taken here may serve as a guide for others undertaking microbiome studies of low-biomass environments, particularly when considering study design, types of controls, and analytical approaches (O'Callaghan et al., 2020).
evidence: Involves speculative reasoning about the broader applicability of the study methods

claim: The sample size is among the largest in microbiome studies of low-biomass sites.
source: The sample size is among the largest in microbiome studies of low-biomass sites, which is helpful in differentiating signal from the noise in this setting.
evidence: Based on comparison with previous studies in the field

claim: All previous microbiome studies that included fallopian tube as a study site had less than 40 patients in each group.
source: All previous microbiome studies that included FT as a study site had less than 40 patients in each group (Miles et al., 2017; Brewster et al., 2022; Asangba et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miles et al., 2017; Brewster et al., 2022; Asangba et al., 2023

claim: Due to the cross-sectional nature of the study, there is limited ability to link specific bacteria to ovarian carcinogenesis.
source: Due to the cross-sectional nature of the study, we have limited ability to link specific bacteria to ovarian carcinogenesis, as we would need to demonstrate that exposure to bacteria precedes the cancer.
evidence: Acknowledges the limitation of the study design

claim: Identifying associations between fallopian tube microbiota and ovarian cancer is a critical first step.
source: However, identifying associations between FT microbiota and OC is a critical first step.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about the progression of scientific investigation

claim: The samples were processed in five batches and sequenced on four plates.
source: Due to the large sample size, we processed the samples in five batches and sequenced the libraries on four plates.
evidence: Directly stated as a study characteristic

claim: Cervical samples were separated from low-biomass samples on different sequencing plates to prevent cross-contamination.
source: Even though we separated the cervical samples with the low-biomass samples on different sequencing plates to prevent cross-contamination, we sequenced the low-biomass samples on three different sequencing plates, which could introduce bias due to batch effects.
evidence: Directly stated as a study design element

claim: Sequencing low-biomass samples on three different sequencing plates could introduce bias due to batch effects.
source: Even though we separated the cervical samples with the low-biomass samples on different sequencing plates to prevent cross-contamination, we sequenced the low-biomass samples on three different sequencing plates, which could introduce bias due to batch effects.
